detail: supported
The distinction is defined by the direction of the mapping between the data space and the image space [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the distinction (between object-space and image-space tasks) is defined by the direction of the mapping between the data space and the image space. Source [S1] explicitly defines object-space tasks as involving 'forward mapping' of data toward the screen and image-space tasks as involving 'reverse mapping' of a pixel into the data. Therefore, the evidence directly supports the claim.
supported
The data is already partially sorted due to its organization into macros and distribution among nodes [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that data is partially sorted due to its organization into macros and distribution among nodes. The provided text from Source [S1] explicitly contains the sentence: 'It is important to note that the data is already partially sorted due to its organization into macros and distribution among nodes.' Therefore, every fact in the claim is directly supported by the evidence.
supported
In image-space parallelism, tasks are performed per screen element (pixel or ray) [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that in image-space parallelism, tasks are performed per screen element (pixel or ray). The provided text from Source [S1] explicitly states: 'Image-space tasks are performed per screen element (pixel or ray); a reverse mapping of a pixel into the data at a node.' This directly supports the claim.
supported
This is a reverse mapping of a pixel into the data at a node [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that image-space tasks involve a 'reverse mapping of a pixel into the data at a node'. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states: 'Image-space tasks are performed per screen element (pixel or ray); a reverse mapping of a pixel into the data at a node.' The claim is a direct paraphrase of this sentence found in the evidence.
supported

It separates **Object-Space Parallelism**, which processes data regardless of its projection, from **Image-Space Parallelism**, which processes pixels by mapping them back into the data [S1, unofficial].

The claim accurately reflects the definitions provided in Source [S1]. The source explicitly states that object-space tasks are performed per macro regardless of the data's projection (forward mapping), while image-space tasks are performed per screen element via reverse mapping of a pixel into the data. This matches the claim's description of separating Object-Space Parallelism (processing data regardless of projection) from Image-Space Parallelism (processing pixels by mapping them back into the data).
supported

The specific definitions of forward mapping (data to screen) and reverse mapping (pixel to data) as the basis for task organization are attributed to Westover (1990) and elaborated upon in the taxonomy of algorithms for multicomputers [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that object-space tasks involve a 'forward mapping (Westover '90] of the data toward the screen projection' and image-space tasks involve a 'reverse mapping of a pixel into the data'. This directly supports the claim that these specific definitions are attributed to Westover (1990) and form the basis for the described task organization.
supported
